summaries.example: Imagine a treasure hunt. You know that one clue is true, and you use it to learn something new. Logic asks whether the next step really follows from the clue. Avicenna also studied sentences such as “If the sun rises, then it is day” and “A number is either even or odd.”
summaries.summary: Ibn Sina, also called Avicenna, was a major logician in the Arabic tradition. He learned from Aristotle and earlier thinkers, but he created many new ways to organize and study logic. For Avicenna, logic is a set of tools for avoiding mistakes when we reason. Reasoning means using what is already known to learn something unknown. He separated having an idea, such as the idea of a triangle, from judging that a sentence is true, such as “Every triangle has three sides.” He studied categorical propositions, which connect a subject and a predicate, and hypothetical propositions, which connect whole statements with “if” or “either...or.” He paid special attention to quantity, time, necessity, and possibility. He also developed rules for syllogisms, or arguments made from premises and a conclusion. His work explains how arguments can prove things, how scientific knowledge can be organized, and how fallacies can mislead us.
key_ideas: Avicenna followed ideas from Aristotle but changed and expanded them so greatly that later Arabic logic became largely Avicennan.
He divided statements into categorical forms and hypothetical forms, including “if...then” and “either...or” statements.
He studied time and possibility. A statement might be true always, sometimes, necessarily, or possibly.
He used logic both as a tool for other subjects and as a subject with its own rules.
Good arguments should lead from known ideas to new knowledge, while fallacies are arguments that seem good but contain a mistake.
summaries.why_it_matters: Avicenna shows that logic is more than memorizing debate tricks. It can help people check explanations, distinguish strong reasons from weak ones, and understand how science builds knowledge. His work also matters because it became a major turning point: later Arabic logicians often responded to him by following, changing, or criticizing his ideas.

important_terms.definition: A careful way of thinking that helps us move from things we know to things we do not yet know.
A sentence that can be judged true or false, such as “The sun has risen.”
A statement with a subject and something said about that subject, such as “Every triangle is a shape.”
A statement built from other statements using words such as “if” or “either...or.”
A reasoned argument in which premises are used to reach a conclusion.
Knowing that a statement must be true because it follows from good reasons.

questions_to_think_about: When does a conclusion really follow from a reason?
Can a statement be true sometimes but not always?
Why might “if” and “either...or” need different rules?
What makes an argument look correct even when it is not?

summaries.example: Consider the argument: Every large quantity is countable; every countable thing is either even or odd; therefore every large quantity is either even or odd. Avicenna treats this as a form of reasoning involving a categorical statement and a disjunction. Its success depends not merely on the words used, but on how the terms and propositions are arranged.
summaries.summary: Ibn Sina’s logic is an ambitious reconstruction of the Aristotelian logical tradition. Avicenna treats logic as both a normative instrument for every discipline and a philosophical science with its own subject matter. Its central task is to guide reasoning from known to unknown while preventing error. The foundations of his account are the difference between conception and assertion and the study of higher-order notions such as subject, predicate, proposition, genus, and syllogism. His propositional theory substantially revises traditional Aristotelian analysis. Categorical propositions receive classifications by quantity, quality, temporal and alethic modality, and by referential/substantial versus descriptional readings. Hypothetical propositions are divided into conditionals and disjunctions, with detailed accounts of quantification, following, conflict, contradiction, conversion, and truth conditions. Avicenna then develops categorical and hypothetical syllogistic, including connective arguments, repetitive arguments such as modus ponens and modus tollens, and reductio ad absurdum. In his theory of demonstration, certainty is transferred from premises to conclusions, while definitions supply the conceptions needed by science. His account of per se predication distinguishes essential attributes from necessary but non-essential consequences, helping explain why some demonstrations merely establish that a fact holds whereas others explain why it holds. Finally, his treatment of fallacies classifies errors arising from argument form, subject matter, and language.
key_ideas: Avicenna inherits an Aristotelian framework but reorganizes it so thoroughly that Arabic logic is often described as pre-Avicennan and post-Avicennan.
Logic has both formal and material dimensions: it studies structures of propositions and arguments, but also the kinds of terms and premises that make an argument demonstrative or explanatory.
His distinction between conception and assertion links definitions with concepts and syllogisms with truth and reasoning.

Categorical propositions are analyzed through quantity and quality, explicit or implicit modality, and two readings: one focused on the continued existence of the referent and another on the time it is described by the subject term.

Hypotheticals include conditionals and disjunctions. Conditionals may express necessary following or mere coincidence, while disjunctions may be exclusive and exhaustive, exclusive but non-exhaustive, or inclusive.

Demonstration is the culmination of logic because it explains certainty, definitions, scientific principles, the organization of sciences, and the difference between proving that something is so and explaining why.
summaries.why_it_matters: Avicenna’s system matters historically and philosophically because it is not a passive transmission of Aristotle. It creates a new center of gravity for Arabic logic and supplies later thinkers with a detailed vocabulary for modality, inference, scientific proof, and fallacy. It also raises enduring questions: how should logical form interact with meaning, how do necessity and time affect truth, and what distinguishes a valid inference from a genuinely explanatory demonstration?

important_terms.definition: A theoretical discipline that gives rules for avoiding error in reasoning and for moving legitimately from what is known to what is unknown.
Knowledge of an individual notion or concept, as opposed to judging that a statement is true.
Judging or asserting that a proposition is true; in demonstration, certainty involves justified belief that it cannot be otherwise.
An atomic subject–predicate proposition, analyzed by its quantity, quality, time, and modality.
A compound proposition whose parts are connected conditionally or disjunctively.
An argument form in which premises yield a conclusion, often through a shared middle term or shared proposition.
A qualification concerning such features as necessity, possibility, or time; Avicenna treats every categorical proposition as modalized either explicitly or implicitly.
A proof that establishes that something is the case, especially by transferring certainty from premises to a conclusion.

questions_to_think_about: Why does Avicenna think that the time or condition under which a subject is described can change the logical meaning of a proposition?
How does an implicative conditional differ from one that merely reports two statements occurring together?
Why might the contradictory of “Always, if A, then B” concern the whole conditional relation rather than simply denying B?
Can formal rules by themselves guarantee a scientific explanation, or do the terms and premises also matter?
Why would a theory of fallacies need to examine both the form of an argument and the meanings of its words?

summaries.example: Suppose a teacher says, “If the school bell rings, class ends.” This could mean that the bell is what makes class end, or it could merely report that the two events usually occur together. Avicenna’s logic asks us to notice that difference. He also asks whether the rule holds every time, only sometimes, or under particular conditions.
summaries.summary: Ibn Sina, known in many sources as Avicenna, transformed the logic he inherited from Aristotle and the later Peripatetic tradition. He understood logic as a discipline that helps people avoid errors and move from known information to unknown conclusions. It is also part of philosophy, with its own subject matter. A key starting point is the difference between conception and assertion. Conception is grasping an idea; assertion is judging that a statement is true. This distinction connects definitions with concepts and arguments with truth. Avicenna studied categorical propositions, which have subjects and predicates, and hypothetical propositions, which join statements through conditionals or disjunctions. He examined their quantity, quality, time, necessity, possibility, contradiction, and conversion. One especially important innovation is his use of two readings of categorical statements: one concerns the thing picked out by the subject as long as it exists, while the other concerns it as long as it has the description named by the subject. Avicenna also developed a large theory of syllogisms, including categorical and hypothetical forms, arguments by repeating a part of a conditional, and reductio ad absurdum. In scientific reasoning, demonstrations should produce certainty, and definitions should identify the concepts needed for inquiry. His discussion of fallacies explains how errors can arise from an argument’s structure, its subject matter, or ambiguous language.
key_ideas: Avicenna built on Aristotle and other earlier thinkers, but his innovations made him the leading reference point for much later Arabic logic.
He said logic helps us gain new knowledge from known information and has both a practical role and its own organized subject matter.
He distinguished concepts from judgments: knowing what “triangle” means is different from judging that every triangle has a certain property.
Categorical statements and hypothetical statements need different kinds of analysis. Hypotheticals include conditionals and several kinds of disjunction.
Avicenna made time, necessity, and possibility central to propositions. He also distinguished talking about an object while it exists from talking about it while it has a particular description.
His syllogistic includes ordinary term-based arguments, arguments using whole propositions, proof by contradiction, and rules for identifying fallacies.
summaries.why_it_matters: Avicenna’s logic matters because it shows how a thinker can inherit an old system while reshaping it for new questions. His work influenced later Arabic logic and gave later philosophers tools for analyzing possibility, necessity, scientific proof, and misleading arguments. It also helps us see that reasoning depends on more than a conclusion: we must examine the structure, meanings, conditions, and strength of the premises.

important_terms.definition: A system of rules for reasoning correctly and avoiding mistakes.
Having an idea or concept, such as the idea of a triangle, without yet saying that a sentence about it is true.
Making a judgment that a statement is true or false.
A subject-and-predicate statement, such as “Every bird is an animal” or “Some birds cannot fly.”
A statement made from other statements, usually with “if...then” or “either...or.”
An argument with premises that are meant to support a conclusion.
A feature such as necessity, possibility, or time that qualifies a statement.
A mistake in reasoning that can make a bad argument look convincing.

questions_to_think_about: Is “If it rains, the ground gets wet” a necessary connection or just a pattern that often occurs?
Why might “Some” and “Every” change whether an argument works?
What is the difference between knowing what something is and knowing that a claim about it is true?
Can an argument have a good-looking pattern but still fail because its terms or premises are unsuitable?
Why would a scientist need both valid reasoning and definitions of the things being studied?
